content_html:
Memory - Replay vs Statistical Reconstruction

Does memory in the brain use ‘statistical reconstruction of meaning’?

The brain constructs the most plausible memory given partial traces and current goals. This statistical reconstruction of meaning explains both flexibility and error.

Memory as Replay Memory as Statistical Reconstruction
Assumes a literal, stored “recording” that is played back unchanged. Assumes distributed traces that are recombined using schemas, expectations, and current context.
Accuracy is mainly a function of storage quality. Accuracy is probabilistic; recall is a best‑fit inference given cues and priors.
Errors are noise or decay. Errors (false memories, biases) are by‑products of a generative system optimised for prediction and meaning.
Hippocampus as a “tape head.” Hippocampus binds/disambiguates patterns; cortex stores features; reactivation reconstructs an episode.
Context plays a small role. Context (internal state, cues, culture) is central to what is reconstructed.
Implies fixed “truth” inside memory. Supports multiple plausible recollections depending on goal and perspective.

Recall is generative: cues trigger partial reactivation; schemas/emotions statistically fill gaps; evaluation sets confidence and can modify the stored traces (reconsolidation).

Examples & Evidence

Phenomenon What It Shows Why It Supports Reconstruction
False memories / suggestibility People confidently recall events that never occurred. Generative filling guided by schemas and social cues (Schacter).
State‑dependent recall Mood or context shifts what is remembered. Meaning depends on internal state; recall is conditional, not fixed.
Retrograde amnesia gradients Recent episodic memories are fragile; older ones more semanticised. Hippocampal binding and cortical consolidation dynamics (Nadel & Moscovitch).
Predictive coding in perception Brain uses priors to interpret noisy input. Same circuitry supports “prediction of the past” during recall (Hohwy).
